title: Why Sridhar Vembu Left California for a Village in Tenkasi
dek: In October 2019 Zoho's founder moved from the Bay Area to Mathalamparai to lead a plan for small rural offices, months before a pandemic sent his engineers home.

story.event: Moving from the Bay Area to Mathalamparai village to lead Zoho's rural offices
story.summary: In October 2019 Sridhar Vembu, founder and chief executive of the privately owned software company Zoho, moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to Mathalamparai, a village in Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi district where Zoho had run an office since 2011, saying that to start small rural satellite offices he had to live in a village himself. During the 2020 lockdown Zoho opened more than a dozen rural offices in Tamil Nadu, and by February 2021 had 15.
paragraphs: Most working days in 2020 began for Sridhar Vembu at 4 am, with calls to Zoho's offices in the United States. He made them from his home in Mathalamparai, a farming village below the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi district. By six he was out on a long walk, and some mornings he swam in the village well. Until October 2019 the founder and chief executive of Zoho, a software company he had co-founded as AdventNet in 1996, had lived in California's Bay Area.

The village was not new to the company. In 2011 Zoho had bought four acres there and started with six people in a thatched shed; by 2017 about 200 worked there, and products such as Zoho Desk were built on site. Zoho had grown without outside investors, a freedom Forbes India linked to decisions like this one. Vembu had long thought migration from villages to cities was "not a good idea," he said. A year or two before the move he resolved to open small satellite offices of 10 to 20 people in villages, and decided that to lead them he would have to "set myself up in the village, too." Not everyone was persuaded: the investor Mohandas Pai argued that young people would keep moving to cities, where there were more employers to choose from.

Vembu could not have known what was coming. Zoho closed its offices two weeks before the government announced a national lockdown, co-founder Shailesh Kumar Davey said, because Vembu wanted staff home before trains, buses and airports filled with panic. During the lockdown the company opened more than a dozen small offices in rural Tamil Nadu so engineers could work near their families. "My only demand was to set up offices in rural areas. They decided the locations," Vembu said. By February 2021 there were 15, with at least 25 planned by the end of that year.

The village changed his own days too. In 2020 he began tutoring three children; within six months there were 52 pupils, mostly children of farm labourers, and four teachers, and by early 2021 about 120. "Where we create jobs is where people flock," he told the Deccan Herald.

quote.text: He who would seek for a stray child, but will not leave his home, is like to lose him.
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Zhuangzi aimed the line at a rival who searched for the Way without ever leaving his own school. Vembu applied the same logic to geography: if the people he hoped to find and keep were in the villages, he could not lead that search from California.

reflection: Vembu did not ask engineers to go back to their districts while he stayed in California. He moved first, months before anyone knew a pandemic would make the idea look obvious, and the offices that followed were placed where employees chose to live. Whether rural offices can hold young people against the pull of cities is still argued.

Zhuangzi's point reaches past geography. The people you most need to understand, a colleague, a customer, someone at home, are easier to know in their own setting than in yours. Going to them costs time, and it usually repays it.
invitation: Choose one person whose work you depend on but rarely see in their own setting. Ask if you can spend half an hour where they work this week, and mostly watch.

cross_checks.claim: Vembu moved from the Bay Area to Mathalamparai in Tenkasi district in late 2019 (October by most accounts).
Zoho's Mathalamparai office opened in 2011 with about six people.
Vembu said the move was so he could lead small rural offices himself, and that the pandemic was not foreseen when he moved.
During the 2020 lockdown Zoho opened more than a dozen rural offices, reaching 15 by February 2021.
Vembu's tutoring of three children grew into a school of 52 pupils by October 2020 and about 120 by February 2021.
Zoho grew without venture capital and is privately owned, mostly by Vembu and his family.

research_notes: Date of the move: Forbes India (June 2020) and the Hindustan Times (February 2021) say October 2019; the Deccan Herald (February 2021) says November 2019; The News Minute says late 2019. The story uses October 2019. Start of the Tenkasi office: The Week (2025) says six employees in a thatched-roof shed in 2011, Outlook Business a six-member team, DT Next (IANS) 'hardly 10'; the story uses six. Headcount at Mathalamparai is not given for 2019-20 because figures disagree (about 200 in 2017 per Forbes India; 500 across Tenkasi and Renigunta in mid-2020 per Forbes India; 450 per the Hindustan Times in 2021; 750, about 900 and 1,200 in later reports); the story cites only the 2017 figure. The Hindustan Times also says 90 per cent of Zoho's roughly 9,000 staff were in rural centres, which contradicts Forbes India's 500 of 9,300 and is not used. Rural centres: the Indian Express (October 2020) says over a dozen opened during the lockdown; the Deccan Herald (February 2021) quotes Vembu saying 15, with at least 25 planned for the end of 2021. School: 52 pupils and four teachers in October 2020 (Indian Express), 120 in February 2021 (Deccan Herald). Funding: Forbes India (2017) says Zoho was built without venture capital or other outside money; The News Minute says 88 per cent is owned by Vembu and his family; the 'bootstrapped' label rests on these. The link between that independence and the Tenkasi decision is Forbes India's framing and is attributed to it. 'Set myself up in the village, too' and 'not a good idea' are from Vembu's May 2020 Forbes India interview, so they are near-contemporary rather than hindsight. Zhuangzi's line comes in a passage where Chuang Tzu criticises Hui Tzu's narrow search for Tao; it is applied here by analogy.
